body: Toronto home sales just posted their biggest monthly jump in 10 months, even while prices kept drifting lower.   So no, the market is not “fixed.”  But it is also not dead.  This looks more like a reset than a collapse:  Sellers are losing some power. Buyers are getting more room. Lenders are asking better questions. And fake-good deals are getting exposed.  Canada’s economy is weak enough for caution, but not broken enough for panic. Even the Bank of Canada warned against obsessing over the “technical recession” headline because April GDP was already showing a rebound.   That is the market now.  Not boom. Not crash. Just a market where the easy money is gone — and structure matters again.  The shortcuts disappeared. The deals did not.

Because sometimes the biggest thing you build isn’t the business. It’s the mindset your kids inherit long after everything else is gone  New dad. Small-time operator. Recent immigrant.  Five years ago he came to Canada chasing a better future.  Now he was trying to buy a trucking company built over 50 years.  Not exactly the industry most people are rushing into right now.  And not exactly a deal most lenders immediately understand either.  The ask: $2.2M.  The structure ended up being a mix of institutional financing and equipment leases secured against plant, property, equipment, and receivables — with room to keep a VTB in second position.  But this wasn’t really a story about trucks.   It was about leaving your kids more than a business to inherit. :)

Commercial credit is finally starting to feel pre-tightening again.  With the Bank of Canada back down at 2.25% after two cuts in 2025, A-class files are now clearing with all-in coupons starting around 4% again — especially on clean, well-leased assets. ￼  Meanwhile, the big-bank “black holes” aren’t so black anymore. RBC just posted record $20.4B profit and is still stuffing reserves for future loan losses — which means they’re being picky on anything that isn’t perfect, and a lot of deals are getting kicked out to the rest of the market. ￼  Layer on top of that a U.S.-led tariff mess and slower housing numbers, and Canada needs cheaper, smarter commercial money to keep real projects moving. ￼  That’s where we live: 	•	Rates starting 4% on strong commercial / institutional files 	•	60+ lenders (not just the usual 5 banks) 	•	Fees under 1% 	•	Private second? Still not a problem.  Commercial debt is being repriced in real time. You can either accept the first offer… or make 60 lenders compete for you.

Luxury on Sale? Or on Life Support?  Canadian fashion giant Ssense has filed for creditor protection (CCAA) after U.S. tariffs and tighter financing squeezed its margins. Once a global go-to for luxury, it now survives on $40M interim financing and a court-approved restructuring, while creditors push for a sale.  👜 For shoppers: rare deep discounts. ⚖️ For employees: uncertainty. 📉 For Canada: a warning on luxury retail’s fragility.  But Ssense isn’t alone. Globally, luxury is wobbling:  • Bain forecasts contraction of –2% to –5% (and up to –9% in a worst-case).  • Gen Z buyers are demanding value and authenticity, not endless price hikes.  • In the U.S., luxury retail grew in early 2025, but inflation and tariffs cloud the outlook.  • LuxExperience (NET-A-PORTER, MR PORTER) just cut 700 jobs in a restructuring wave.  👉 What looks like a “Canadian problem”  could really be a macro story: tariffs, financing costs, and shifting consumer sentiment are squeezing luxury worldwide.  The fallout? Deals for shoppers, layoffs for workers, and a reshaping of what “luxury” means in 2025  📚 Sources: Vogue Business, WWD, The Logic, BetaKit, WSJ, Bain & Co., Reuters, Fashion Network, Business Insider.

Canada is building for renters. But what if the renters don’t come back?  CMHC says Canada’s 2025 housing starts rose 6%, driven by record rental construction and expanding missing-middle housing. Source: CMHC  For years, the rental market had one simple assumption:  More students. More workers. More newcomers. More demand.  But that story is changing.  Canada is reducing temporary resident targets and aiming to bring non-permanent residents below 5% of the population by the end of 2027. Source: Government of Canada / IRCC  Temporary resident inflows are slowing, and RBC says rising rental supply could keep apartment rent growth in check. Source: RBC Economics  CBRE expects 2026 to be a transition year for multifamily, with softer demand and new supply pushing vacancy rates higher. Source: CBRE Canada  Rents are already showing weakness, with national asking rents continuing to decline year-over-year. Source: Rentals.ca & Urbanation  So the uncomfortable question is:  Who rents all the new units?  If demand doesn’t bounce back, everything changes:  Rents. Vacancy. Cash flow. Refinancing. Pre-con exits. Investor appetite.  The old market rewarded waiting.  This one rewards better math.  Think mortgages? Think TheRateFinder.ca

A 34-unit apartment project in Edmonton has been placed into receivership.  The project was financed through a first mortgage bridge facility. The loan matured on March 1 with approximately $4.2M outstanding.  A site inspection prior to the appointment noted that construction had stopped, with significant work still incomplete.  A registered construction lien by the contractor further constrained the borrower’s ability to refinance or complete the project.  KSV has been  appointed as receiver, March 13.  #receiver #receivership #receivershipready

These are the homes that typically create naturally affordable housing — duplexes, triplexes, 4–10 unit buildings  A typical 6–7 unit project needs roughly $2.3M in loans. Too small for large banks to prioritize. Too complex for their margins.  These projects require real work — draw schedules, holdbacks, quantity surveyors.  Smaller banks and credit unions should fill the gap. But most aren’t licensed, structured, or permitted to do construction financing at scale.  So capital moves elsewhere.  Private lenders step in. Rates rise. Friction follows.  Until financing fits this scale, the middle stays missing.
